idiom_name: mutable.Map per scope plus a parent chain (or an immutable Map chain threaded through the walk)
implementation_notes: Scala's collections make both shapes short - an imperative scope stack of mutable.Map[String, Symbol] frames with a reverse walk for lookup, or a purely functional chain of immutable Maps threaded through the traversal - but the pattern itself is still hand-written: you decide which constructs open scopes, when symbols are defined and how uses resolve. What replaces the classic structure is mutable.Map/ArrayDeque (or List[Map[...]] in the functional form) plus case class or enum entries; scalac's own scala.reflect.internal.Scopes shows the classic shape at compiler scale (Scope/ScopeEntry hash buckets with nesting levels), and Scala 3 replaced the static table with phase-indexed Denotations resolved through prefix.member(name) - both are compiler internals, not reusable libraries. Keep the hand-written table for your language or DSL, and prefer the immutable-chain form when the resolver is functional and scopes must be shared without mutation.
pitfalls: scala.collection.mutable.Map is not thread-safe and is invariant in its key type: keys must be String (or one interned wrapper type) consistently, and a resolver shared across parallel phases needs synchronization or an immutable snapshot.
Implicit and given resolution is a second lookup layer with its own nesting rules: a resolver that only handles term names will not model the language's real binding behaviour.

Exhaustive matching on symbol kinds is only guaranteed for a closed ADT (enum/sealed trait): string kinds or Option[Any] lose the exhaustiveness check and turn resolution bugs into MatchError at runtime.
